questions.q: What makes the Zune a different kind of failure from the Edsel or the Newton?
options: The Zune's technology was badly broken at launch
The Zune was a competent, well-designed product that failed because of a flawed process around it, not the product itself
The Zune was never actually released to the public
The Zune had no real competitors in the market
questions.explanation: The Zune HD was genuinely good and well reviewed — some people preferred it to the iPod Touch. Its failure came from a flawed design process: unclear purpose, mis-targeted marketing, missing stakeholders and bad timing, not from the product being poor.

questions.q: For an innovation to be successful, it must
options: be advertised effectively.
address the needs of users.
have a registered trademark.
be launched at an appropriate time.
questions.explanation: A successful innovation must meet a genuine user need, otherwise consumers will not adopt it regardless of marketing. Advertising, trademarks and timing can support an innovation but cannot make a product succeed if it fails to address user needs — for most buyers the Zune offered no real reason to switch from the iPod.

questions.q: Which combination of factors most influences the success of an innovation?
options: Social demand and cultural values
Product demand and social implications
Timing and appropriate marketing strategies
Ease of use and economical manufacturing processes
questions.explanation: The success of an innovation depends largely on timing — releasing the product when the market is ready — combined with appropriate marketing strategies to reach consumers. The Zune was both mistimed (smartphones were swallowing the market) and poorly marketed (artsy, niche advertising), so even a strong device failed.

questions.q: Which of the following factors has the most significant effect on the success of a marketing plan?
options: The cost of the product
Use of television and radio
Understanding the market segment
Effective packaging and the point of sale
questions.explanation: A marketing plan succeeds when it is built on a clear understanding of the target market segment, because that knowledge shapes pricing, advertising and packaging decisions. Microsoft marketed a mainstream product as if it were a niche one and missed the broad audience of ordinary listeners who were buying iPods.

questions.q: Which stakeholder did Microsoft fail to properly involve when developing the Zune, and with what effect?
options: Retail stores, so the Zune was never sold in shops
The music industry, so features that could have been negotiated were simply blocked
Software developers, so the device had no third-party apps
Government regulators, so the device was banned from sale
questions.explanation: Microsoft needed the record labels on side to give itself leverage against Apple, but neglected those relationships. Involving the right stakeholders early is part of a good design process; leaving the music industry out meant negotiable features were blocked.

questions.q: Which of the following best indicates that a product is becoming obsolete?
options: When innovative design features are incorporated
When the product has been superseded by a newer design
When there is a decrease in the product's sales and turnover
When the product has undergone modifications to improve its function
questions.explanation: Obsolescence occurs when a product is superseded by a newer or improved design and is no longer wanted. The whole category of standalone music players was being superseded by smartphones that played music, took photos and did everything else — a shift the Zune could not out-design.

questions.q: From memory: list the three main reasons the episode gives for why the Zune failed despite being a good product.
keyPoints: A fuzzy design process produced confused marketing with no clear target — it sold a mainstream product as a niche one.
The wrong stakeholders were left out — Microsoft neglected the music industry, so negotiable features were blocked.
Bad timing and momentum — smartphones were about to eat the whole standalone-player market, and Apple's marketing power was an overwhelming wall.
questions.explanation: If you recalled all three — mis-targeted marketing, missing stakeholders, and late-to-a-shifting-market timing — grade yourself Good or Easy. The lesson is that a well-made product can still fail if the process around it is broken.

questions.q: In your own words: how did a lack of clarity at the top of the design process flow down and hurt the Zune?
keyPoints: The marketing team never got a clear picture of what the Zune was or who it was for.
When a design process lacks clarity at the top, downstream people can't do their jobs.
The result was artsy, narrow advertising that missed the broad mass of ordinary music listeners buying iPods.
questions.explanation: The key idea is that clarity of purpose must be set early in the design process — without it, even a capable marketing team produces a campaign aimed at the wrong audience.

questions.q: Explain how marketing and the design process contributed to the failure of the Microsoft Zune. (4 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: The Zune failed largely because the design process lacked clarity at the top: the marketing team never got a clear picture of what the product was or who it was for. When a design process is fuzzy in this way, the people downstream cannot do their jobs effectively. As a result, the Zune's advertising was artsy and aimed at a very narrow, specific audience, marketing a mainstream product as if it were niche. This missed the broad mass of ordinary music listeners — the very people who were actually buying iPods — so even a competent, well-designed device failed to sell.

criteria.descriptor: Identifies that the design process lacked clarity about what the Zune was and who it was for.
Links unclear purpose at the top of the process to downstream teams being unable to do their jobs.
Describes the marketing as artsy/niche and aimed at the wrong, narrow audience.
Concludes that mis-targeting the mainstream iPod audience contributed to the product's failure.

questions.explanation: The crux is connecting a fuzzy design process to mis-targeted marketing: a mainstream product was sold as a niche one, so it missed its real market.

questions.q:
Question 14 (15 marks)

Analyse factors that could determine the success or failure of an innovative design.

Your answer will be assessed on how well you: demonstrate knowledge and understanding relevant to the question; communicate ideas and information using relevant examples; and present a logical and cohesive response.
questions.modelAnswer: Several factors determine whether an innovative design succeeds or fails. Successes can be driven by timing (releasing a product aligned to a seasonal change so it matches perceived consumer needs), social factors (the rising demand for meal-kit food products reflecting society's desire for convenience), and political support (government STEM-education initiatives that drive innovation). Failures can stem from available technologies (an innovation needing newer supporting technology to work, such as moving from wired headphones to Bluetooth), cultural factors (designing without considering consumers' cultural needs, e.g. supplying high technology to communities that lack electrical power), and marketing strategies (over-promising operational qualities, as with vehicle safety features recalled after causing injury). Function and aesthetics are also decisive: an electric car's batteries must meet drivers' range needs to be judged successful, while the latest phones must both look good and display information attractively (e.g. wrap-around screens) or consumers will turn to competitors. A strong response analyses how these interacting factors combine to determine the success or failure of the innovation.

criteria.descriptor: Shows a comprehensive understanding of factors that help determine the success or failure of an innovative design; draws out and relates implications of those factors; provides a logical and cohesive response supported by relevant examples
Explains how factors help determine the success or failure of an innovative design; communicates using relevant examples; provides a mostly logical and cohesive response
Describes factors that determine the success or failure of an innovative design; provides a mostly organised response, supported by relevant example(s)
Outlines factors that determine the success or failure of an innovative design; provides example(s)
Demonstrates some understanding of factors that determine the success or failure of an innovative design

questions.explanation: This is a real HSC extended-response question. The Zune is an ideal worked example: a competent product undone by mistimed release, mis-targeted marketing and missing stakeholders — exactly the interacting factors the question asks you to analyse.
